title: Paris Agreement

definition.text: An international climate treaty, negotiated in 2015 and signed in 2016, covering mitigation, adaptation and finance.

facts.text: It aims to keep warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and preferably to 1.5 °C, with emissions reaching net zero by mid-century.
It was negotiated by 196 parties at the 2015 UN climate conference near Paris and entered into force on 4 November 2016.
Each country sets its own contributions, and each new target should go beyond the last, though nothing forces a country to set a specific target.
Unlike the Kyoto Protocol, it blurs the line between developed and developing countries, so developing countries must also submit emission-cut plans.
The EU and 194 states, covering over 98% of greenhouse gas emissions, have ratified or joined it; the United States withdrew in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and withdrew again in 2026.
It recognises loss and damage as a separate pillar, but states it cannot be used as a basis for liability.
Global emissions kept rising after it was signed, and most experts say it is insufficient for its 1.5 °C goal.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

title: Effectiveness of the Paris Agreement

definition.text: The debate over whether the Paris Agreement can achieve its temperature goals.

facts.text: Most experts say it is insufficient for the 1.5 °C goal, though some argue it is too early to judge.
UNEP said in 2020 that current commitments would likely lead to more than 3 °C of warming by 2100.
Studies in Nature found that as of 2017 none of the major industrialised nations was implementing its pledged policies.
The stocktake report credits it with a large effect: the expected 2100 warming fell from 3.7–4.8 °C in 2010 to 2.4–2.6 °C at COP 27.

contested_note: Most experts judge the agreement insufficient for 1.5 °C, while others point to the drop in projected warming since it was adopted.

definition.text: The Paris Agreement's common system, under Article 13, for monitoring, reporting and verifying what countries do on climate and the support they give or receive.

facts.text: Parties are legally bound to have their progress toward their NDCs checked by technical expert review.
Developed and developing countries alike report every two years and face technical and peer review.
It has built-in flexibility in scope, detail and frequency of reporting for countries with less capacity.

definition.text: The international policy goal of keeping global warming below two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial (1850–1900) levels.

facts.text: It is a political decision based on science about the likely consequences of warming, dating from the 2009 Copenhagen conference, and is central to the Paris Agreement.
It is often criticised as too high, since two degrees of warming would have serious effects on people and nature.
The IPCC's 2018 special report warned that 2 °C rather than 1.5 °C would worsen extreme weather, sea-ice loss, sea-level rise, coral bleaching and ecosystem loss.
The UNFCCC predicts a likely 2.1 to 2.9 °C of warming by 2100, exceeding the target.
An 'overshoot pathway' would pass 2 °C and then bring warming back down by late in the century, requiring management over many decades.

title: Climate club

definition.text: A voluntary coalition of countries that agree on a common climate standard, such as a carbon price, and penalise non-members.

facts.text: Membership is voluntary and excludable, avoiding the need for every country to agree.
Countries join for the shared benefit of lower global emissions and to escape sanctions, such as tariffs, imposed on outsiders.
William Nordhaus pioneered the idea in 2015: members price carbon and charge a fee on imports from countries without similar pricing.
A 2025 Econometrica paper found such a club, with border taxes to deter free-riding, could achieve 33–68% of the globally optimal carbon reduction.
The G7 Climate Club, launched in December 2022, favours partnerships over penalties and had 46 member states as of May 2025.
Exporting countries fearing fees and researchers sceptical of carbon pricing have criticised it; the EU's CBAM has been called a possible first climate club.

contested_note: Critics fear export fees and doubt carbon pricing, while others argue supposed losers such as China and India would gain.
